title: Labels and the table
subtitle: Reading Piedmont and eating with it

steps.title: Reading the label
steps.body: Labels name the DOC or DOCG, like Barolo or Barbera d'Asti, the producer, the vintage and often an MGA or vineyard name. Riserva marks longer ageing. Langhe Nebbiolo and Nebbiolo d'Alba are more affordable Nebbiolos. The DOCG strip on the neck guarantees origin.

steps.title: At the table
steps.body: Piedmont's food is rich: tajarin, thin egg pasta with butter and white truffle; vitello tonnato; brasato al Barolo, beef braised in Barolo; bagna cauda, a hot garlic and anchovy dip. Barolo suits truffles and braised meat; Barbera suits salumi and pasta; Dolcetto suits everyday dishes; Moscato suits hazelnut cake.
steps.highlight: Truffle with Barolo, salumi with Barbera

steps.prompt: Which Piedmont dish is cooked with Barolo?

steps.title: Service
steps.body: Serve Barolo and Barbaresco at 17 to 18 degrees, in large glasses, decanted for hours when young. They're best from 10 years and can age 30 or more. Barbera and Dolcetto at 15 to 17, young. Moscato d'Asti well chilled, at 6 to 8.

steps.explanation: Sorbet is too sweet and acidic.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Labels show DOCG, MGA and Riserva
Barolo suits truffle and braised beef; Barbera suits salumi
Decant young Barolo; it ages 30 years or more
